headline: Full Moon Outgoing: Bass Tuck Into the Deep Hole After Midnight
subhead: With the ocean pushing 79 degrees, the real bite at Shinnecock is happening after the boats go home — in the dark, on the back half of the outgoing.
body_markdown:
I stopped fighting the clock a long time ago. Every August, guys ask me why I'm rigging up at 10pm instead of hitting the inlet at first light, and the answer is simple — right now, first light is the worst time to be there. The ocean's sitting near 79 degrees off the beach, the sun's been baking the flats all afternoon, and every striper with a brain has slid into deep water and gone quiet until the heat breaks. So I wait. I fish the back half of the outgoing, starting a couple hours before the tide bottoms out, when that warm surface water finally starts draining off the flats and the current stacks bait against structure. That's when the inlet wakes up.

This week that meant the deep hole on the ocean side of the jetty, current ripping through by 11pm on a rising moon, and bass showing up right on schedule. Nothing enormous — mostly 26 to 32 inches, with a couple of fish pushing 34 mixed in — but they've been consistent for anyone willing to stand there in the dark and work it right. Livelined bunker under a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold bottom in that current, has been the best producer. Guys throwing bucktails are doing fine too — 1.5-ounce white or bone bucktails, cast up-current and allowed to swing down through the hole before a slow, deliberate retrieve along bottom. The full moon this week has the tide moving with real authority, which sharpens that outgoing bite into a tighter window than usual — you get about ninety minutes of prime current before it goes soft, so don't waste the front end of it fumbling with rigs on the beach.

Inside the bay, fluke are still the most dependable fish going, and the canal remains the smart move if you want a shot without burning half a tank of gas running the ocean side. The lock-driven current at Shinnecock Canal County Park does the work for you — when those gates start opening, bait gets funneled and squeezed, and fluke stack up on that edge for the thirty to forty-five minutes the current's really moving. I've been doing well there with a half-ounce chartreuse bucktail tipped with a 4-inch Gulp swimming mullet, bounced slow along the rubble bottom right where the current narrows. Bring extra rigs — that bottom eats hooks and jig heads, no way around it. Out in the open bay, the drift bite off Tiana and the flats south of the canal has been decent on the last two hours of the incoming, doormats mixing in with the shorts on white Gulp and squid strip combos in 15 to 20 feet, right along the edges where the sandy bottom drops into the deeper channel.

Weakfish at Ponquogue Bridge have been a mixed bag — some nights the current lines up and you get a nice pull of fish holding tight to the pilings on the last of the outgoing, other nights it's dead quiet and you're better off targeting the blues that are sweeping through instead. When it's working, small pink or chartreuse jig heads with a soft plastic shad tail, fished slow and bounced right off the bottom structure near the bridge lights, have been the ticket after dark. The lights themselves matter — weakfish sit in that shadow line where the current brings bait past the pilings, and a well-placed cast into the dark edge beats blind casting into the lit water every time.

Bluefish have been the most reliable fish in the system the past two weeks, honestly — snapper blues are thick in the back bay creeks off Tiana and Hampton Bays proper, giving kids and light-tackle guys steady action on small metal and Kastmasters. The adult blues are showing in sweeps through the inlet itself, usually pushing bait ahead of the tide change, and when they come through it's fast and violent for ten or fifteen minutes before they move on. Keep a rod rigged with a tin ready even when you're fishing for bass — those blues don't wait for you to switch gear.

Looking ahead, this moon-driven current isn't going to hold at this strength much longer. Once we're a few days past full, the tide swings will ease back to something more normal, and that means the bite windows at the inlet and the canal will widen back out a little rather than being crammed into that tight ninety-minute stretch. That's not necessarily bad news — it usually means a more forgiving bite for anyone who can't be out there at exactly the right minute. If the ocean holds in the high 70s like it has, I'd expect the bass to keep favoring the deep hole and current edges after dark rather than pushing onto the flats during the day, so plan around the night tide, not the sunrise. And if that peanut bunker keeps building in the back bay creeks the way it has, don't be surprised if the weakfish bite at the bridge firms up before the month's out — that's the pattern I'd be watching closest over the next couple weeks.
